## Simple explanation

A word embedding represents a word as a list of numbers. Words used in
similar contexts may have vectors that are close to each other.

## Technical explanation

Word embeddings map vocabulary items to dense vectors. They may be learned
from context-prediction objectives, supervised tasks, or as part of a larger
language model. Static embeddings assign one vector per word type, whereas
contextual representations vary with the word's surrounding text.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Embeddings convert discrete tokens into numerical inputs that models can
process. They support semantic generalization, but static word-level
representations can struggle with ambiguity, rare words, and languages with
complex morphology.

## How it works

An embedding table stores one vector per vocabulary ID. Training updates
vectors so that the model's objective is improved; for example, word2vec
learns vectors from context prediction. Modern Transformer models often
combine token embeddings with positional information and contextual layers.

## Practical example

In a language model, token IDs index an embedding matrix to obtain vectors
before the first Transformer block. Inspecting nearest neighbors can reveal
useful structure, but may also expose biases present in training data.

## Common misconceptions

- A word's nearest neighbors reflect the training data and objective, not an
  objective definition of meaning.
- A static word embedding and a contextual token representation are related
  but not identical concepts.
